Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities

Cynthia V. Nguyen, MD (2020–present)
Firoz Miyanji, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the anatomy, pathophysiology and disorders associated with nontraumatic
pediatric cervical spine abnormalities.
Perform an appropriate evaluation of patients in whom cervical spine abnormalities are
suspected, including appropriate imaging studies.
Review the nonsurgical and surgical management of cervical spine abnormalities.
Discuss the potential complications of management of cervical spine abnormalities.
Overview
Nontraumatic abnormalities of the cervical spine are rare in the pediatric population but
important to recognize to prevent potential neurologic injury.
Certain diseases are associated with congenital deformities of the cervical spine.

Anatomy
Development
Atlas (C1)
Develops from three ossification centers: two lateral masses and one body1
Fully fused at age 7 years
Axis (C2)
The tip of the dens is not ossified at birth but appears at aged 3 years and fuses to the dens by
age 12 years.
The odontoid process is separated from the body of the axis by a synchondrosis featuring a
cork-in-a-bottle appearance, which usually fuses by age 6 to 7 years.2
Subaxial Cervical Spine (C3 through C7)
Vertebral bodies are initially wedged shaped, becoming more adult in shape by age 8 years.3
Joints
Atlanto-Occipital Junction
Bony stability with cup-shaped joints between C1 and occipital condyles
Key ligament that stabilizes is the tectorial membrane.4
Atlantoaxial Joint
Very mobile; allows generous head motion
Allows flexion/extension, lateral bending, and rotation
Key ligament that stabilizes the atlantoaxial complex is the transverse ligament, which
represents the thickest, strongest portion of the cruciform ligament.1
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Basilar Invagination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
2/22

Upper cervical spine encroaches on the brainstem and spinal cord as the base of the skull is
displaced toward the cranial vault.5
May cause compression of cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord
Often associated with other osseous anomalies of the craniovertebral junction, including
Klippel-Feil syndrome, occipitocervical synostosis, incomplete ring of C1, and hypoplasia of the
basiocciput, occipital condyles, and atlas6
Also commonly found in patients with systemic disorders, such as achondroplasia,
osteogenesis imperfecta, Morquio syndrome, and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia (Figure 1)
Motor and sensory disturbances occur in 85% of individuals with basilar invagination. Patients
may present with headache, neck ache, and neurologic compromise.2
Figure 1 Images of the cervical spine of a 14-year-old boy with osteogenesis imperfecta. A,
Preoperative sagittal T2-weighted MRI shows progressive basilar invagination B, Postoperative
lateral radiograph demonstrates fusion from the occiput to C2. (Reproduced from Wallace MJ,
Kruse RW, Shah SA: The spine in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2017;25[2]:100-109.)
Occipitocervical Synostosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
3/22

Abnormal bony connection between the occiput and the upper cervical spine; commonly
associated with C2-C3 fusion1
Atlantoaxial instability is present in 50% of patients with synostosis.7
Unilateral Absence of C1
Congenital malformation of the C1 ring; may cause atlantoaxial instability1
Associated with other congenital anomalies, including tracheoesophageal fistula
Odontoid Anomalies
Continuum from aplasia (complete absence) through varying degrees of hypoplasia7 (Figure 2)
Figure 2 Illustration shows the gradations of odontoid anomalies. (Reproduced from Copley
LA, Dormans JP: Cervical spine disorders in infants and children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
1998;6[4]:204-214.)
Os odontoideum is a circumferentially corticated ossicle separated from the body of C2. The
ossicle is an entity distinct from an odontoid fracture or a persistent ossiculum terminale.8
May lead to instability; symptoms may present as nondescript pain or include occipitocervical
pain, myelopathy, or vertebrobasilar ischemia8 (Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
4/22

Figure 3 Lateral flexion radiograph (A) and sagittal CT scan (B) of the cervical spine of a 4-year-old
boy show C1-C2 instability and os odontoideum. (Reproduced from Hedequist DJ, Mo AZ: Os
odontoideum in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2020;28[3]:e100-e107.)
Congenital Muscular Torticollis
Common postural deformity evident shortly after birth, typically characterized by ipsilateral
cervical lateral flexion and contralateral cervical rotation because of unilateral shortening of
the sternocleidomastoid muscle9
Etiology unclear; intrauterine impairment of sternocleidomastoid development9
Ophthalmologic, vestibular, and congenital conditions and trauma and tumors often are
associated and possibly causative. If a tight sternocleidomastoid is not present, other causes
of torticollis should be sought.2
Associated with hip dysplasia and metatarsus adductus
Klippel-Feil Syndrome
Congenital fusion of the cervical spine, ranging from two-segment fusion to involvement of the
entire cervical spine10
Associated with the clinical triad of a short neck, a low posterior hairline, and marked
limitation of range of motion of the neck
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
5/22

Patterns of malformation associated with a high risk of instability are those that limit cervical
motion to one level, including atlanto-occipital fusion with C2-C3 block vertebrae, abnormal
atlanto-occipital junction with several distal block vertebrae, and a single open interspace
between block segments11 (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Preoperative lateral flexion (A) and extension (B) radiographs of the cervical spine of
a 3-year-old child with Klippel-Feil syndrome demonstrate block vertebrae of C2-C3 and
assimilation of C1 with the occiput. The atlantodens interval is grossly widened, indicating
instability of C1-C2. (Reproduced from Wills BP, Dormans JP: Nontraumatic upper cervical
spine instability in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[4]:233-245.)
Associated conditions include congenital scoliosis, renal anomalies, Sprengel deformity
(elevated dysplastic scapula), impaired hearing, synkinesia, and congenital heart disease.
Renal ultrasonography and echocardiography should be performed in these patients.4
Atlantoaxial Rotatory Displacement
Spectrum of pathologic changes ranging from mild displacement to severe displacement and
eventually the fixation of C1 on C2 in a subluxated position1
Etiologies may be varied but usually are trauma or inflammation.12
May result from very mild trauma
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
6/22

Described by Grisel (Grisel syndrome);13 any condition that results in inflammation in the
head or neck may be implicated.
Respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, pharyngitis, mastoiditis, otitis media
Autoimmune disorders
Fielding and Hawkins classification (Figure 5)
Figure 5 Illustrations show the Fielding and Hawkins atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation
classification. Type I, unilateral facet subluxation with intact transverse ligament; no
displacement between the anterior arch of C1 and the dens. Type II, unilateral facet
subluxation with anterior displacement of 3 to 5 mm. Type III, bilateral anterior facet
displacement; the interval between the C1 arch and the dens is >5 mm. Type IV, posterior
displacement of the atlas. (Reproduced from Neal KM, Mohamed AS: Atlantoaxial rotatory
subluxation in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2015;23[6]:382-392.)
Video 1 demonstrates atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation.14
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
7/22

Video 1 Shah SA: C1-C2 fixation for atlantoaxial rotatory instability. Presented at the 14th
Annual International Pediatric Orthopaedic Symposium, Orlando, FL, November 28-
December 2, 2017.
Diseases Associated with Cervical Spine Abnormalities
Down Syndrome
Cervical instability caused by ligamentous laxity15
Instability of C1 on C2 in excess of 5 mm occurs in 14% to 17% of patients.16
Hypoplasia of the posterior arch of C1 may occur in 26% of patients.17
Symptomatic cervical spine instability develops in 3% of patients with Down syndrome.18
Indications for surgical management unclear
Larsen Syndrome
Associated with cervical kyphosis and instability
Imaging studies should be obtained immediately if diagnosed.19
Skeletal Dysplasias
Morquio Syndrome
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
8/22

C1-C2 instability related to odontoid hypoplasia19
Soft-tissue glycosaminoglycan deposits, which cause stenosis and lead to myelopathy17
Pseudoachondroplasia
C1-C2 instability related to odontoid hypoplasia19
Spondyloepiphyseal Dysplasia
High risk of myelopathy because of atlantoaxial instability in addition to underlying stenosis19
Diastrophic Dysplasia
Mid-cervical kyphosis is unique to this patient population and is present in as many as one-
third of all patients.19
Kyphosis less than 60° likely resolves by age 6 years; larger curves are unlikely to resolve.19
Diastrophic dysplasia also is associated with cervical spina bifida occulta.
Autoimmune Disease
Most frequent finding in the cervical spine in patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is
zygapophyseal fusion, which often is asymptomatic.20
Odontoid waist may be eroded because of synovial hypertrophy, making it more susceptible to
fracture.20
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Location, duration, level of pain
Neurologic injury red flags: headache, radiation, numbness/tingling, weakness, loss of
bowel/bladder control, issues with balance or fine motor skills (buttoning)
One of the first signs of myelopathy in children may be gradual loss of physical endurance.4
Past Medical History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
9/22

Conditions associated with cervical spine abnormalities
Other deformities
Physical Examination
Visual inspection
Klippel-Feil: short neck and low posterior hairline
Muscle wasting
Range of motion
Neurologic examination
Strength, sensation, reflexes, spasticity
In young patients, a focused neurologic examination may be difficult. Consider global tests,
such as walking on the tip toes, walk on the heels, or walking in a straight line as on a tight
rope; hopping on one leg; and performing a deep knee squat.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs of the cervical spine primarily include plain AP, lateral, and odontoid views.
Radiographs should be obtained for patients with syndromes associated with cervical
instability.
Obtain flexion-extension views if patient has no history of trauma and a normal physical
examination.4
Pseudosubluxation: physiologic misalignment caused by ligamentous laxity and a more
horizontal orientation of the facet joints in children compared with adults
This anterior displacement manifests on neutral and flexion lateral views and should reduce
on extension.21
Assess via the spinolaminar (Swischuk) line.22 The line should pass within 1.5 mm of the
spinous process of C2 (Figure 6).
Most common at C2-C3 but also observed at C3-C423
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
10/22

Figure 6 Illustration shows the position of the spinolaminar line (Swischuk line), which is used
to determine the presence of pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3. (Reproduced from Copley LA,
Dormans JP: Cervical spine disorders in infants and children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
1998;6[4]:204-214.
Basilar impression/invagination is evaluated on a lateral view and defined by protrusion of
the dens above the McRae line or 5 mm above the McGregor line (Figure 7, A).
Atlantoaxial instability is assessed via the atlanto-dens interval (ADI) and space available for
cord.
Positive if the ADI exceeds 5 mm. Normal ADI in adults is 2 to 3 mm; an ADI of up to 5 mm
may occur in children younger than 8 years who have an intact transverse ligament.
Atlantoaxial instability also is evaluated via the Powers ratio, which is the ratio of the length of
the line from the basion to the posterior margin of the atlas, divided by the distance from the
opisthion to the anterior arch of the atlas (Figure 7, B). A normal Powers ratio is less than 1.0.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
11/22

Figure 7 Illustrations show lateral craniometry. A, The lines commonly used to determine
basilar impression and the measurements for determining atlantoaxial instability are shown.
ADI = atlantodens interval, SAC = space available for cord. B, The Powers ratio is determined by
drawing a line from the basion (B) to the posterior arch of the atlas (C) and then drawing a
second line from the opisthion (O) to the anterior arch of the atlas (A). The length of line BC is
divided by the length of the line OA. A ratio greater than 1.0 is diagnostic of anterior
occipitoatlantal dislocation. (Reproduced from Copley LA, Dormans JP: Cervical spine disorders
in infants and children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[4]:204-214.)
Computed Tomography
CT can be used to confirm the diagnosis and rule out grade III and grade IV atlantoaxial
rotatory displacement, which are associated with neurologic injury and sudden death. In
patients who present acutely and without substantial trauma, limited cuts of C1 and C2 in a
neutral position may confirm the diagnosis with much less radiation than a CT scan of the
entire cervical spine or repeating CT scans with dynamic views.2
CT is vital to plan cervical screw fixation. The course of the vertebral artery may be studied on
a standard CT scan.24
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
12/22

MRI may be useful in evaluating the C1-2 ligamentous complex or if other underlying causes
(infection, tumor) are suspected, without the risk of ionizing radiation.2
Dynamic MRI, in which images are obtained with the cervical spine in flexion and extension,
may confirm spinal cord compression in patients with signs and symptoms suggestive of spine
cord compression who have normal plain radiographs.25
Management
Congenital Muscular Torticollis
Initial management is physical therapy.
Earlier management is associated with better success of physical therapy.9
If no resolution via physical therapy, may consider botulinum toxin injections.
Failed nonsurgical management is an indication for surgical release.
Video 2 Faldini C, Pilla F, Perna F, et al: Congenital Muscular Torticollis: Minimally Invasive Bipolar
Tenotomy [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016.
Atlantoaxial Rotatory Displacement
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
13/22

Duration of symptoms before presentation is the most important predictor of the type of
management required.12
Treatment algorithm is shown in Figure 8.
If present acutely (less than 2 weeks), attempt NSAIDs, rest, and collar immobilization.
If chronic (more than 2 weeks), attempt NSAIDs, halter traction, and muscle relaxants.
If persistent, progress through skeletal traction.
If nonsurgical management fails, surgical management for atlantoaxial instability
Figure 8 Treatment algorithm for atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation. aTime periods for
treatment are variable. bThe definition of acute versus chronic is variable. (Reproduced from
Neal KM, Mohamed AS: Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2015;23[6]:382-392.)
Basilar Invagination
Surgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
14/22

Indication: this is a progressively debilitating condition that, left unmanaged, may result in
profound neurologic deficits and death.24
Before surgical management, consider trial of axial cervical traction to determine reducibility.6
If basilar invagination is not reducible, anterior decompression in combination with posterior
stabilization often is necessary.
Typically managed via fusion from the occiput to C2 or C32
Anterior Surgery
Transoropharyngeal exposure is the most common approach for ventral decompression.
Typically, a subsequent posterior stabilization procedure, which also may include posterior
decompression, is necessary.6
Posterior Surgery
Posterior cervical procedures typically are performed for foramen magnum and posterior
cervical decompression and for stabilization and fusion.
Traditional methods of fixation to the occiput have included rod attachment via wiring/cable
techniques through drill holes in the occiput. Disadvantages of this technique include less than
optimal biomechanical stability and the risk of dural puncture with cable passage.24
Occipital Plating
Occipital morphology can be examined on preoperative CT scans.
Greatest area of thickness lies in the midline of the external occipital protuberance. Screw
placement is best at the external occipital protuberance in the midline.24
Complications may include dural tears from penetration through the inner table.24
Options for fixation to cervical spine include C1-C2 trans-articular screws or C1 lateral mass
screws in combination with C2 pars, pedicle, or laminar screws. Lateral mass screws may be
placed subaxially from C3 to C6 if necessary.6
Cervical Spine Instability
Nonsurgical Management
Sports management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
15/22

Avoid contact sports and sports that require bending, twisting, or axial loading of the neck
(eg, gymnastics, diving).4
Halo Vest
In children, more halo pins (8 to 12) are used at lower insertional torque (1 to 5 ft-lb) compared
with the standard values used in adults (four pins at 6 to 8 ft-lb).1
The complication rate in pediatric patients is high.
Anterior pins most commonly injure the supraorbital nerve.
With halo traction, the sixth cranial (abducens) nerve is the most commonly injured nerve,
which manifests as a loss of lateral gaze. If neurologic injury is noted with halo traction,
traction should be removed.2
Consider halo vest immobilization after fusion in children younger than 8 years because of
their inability to comply with restrictions.24
Surgicall Management
Indications
Neurologic symptoms
More than 10 mm ADI on flexion-extension radiographs.
Persistent pain
In patients with Down syndrome, surgical treatment should be performed if the ADI exceeds 5
mm with neurologic symptoms or exceeds 10 mm without symptoms.
Morquio syndrome and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia: more than 5 mm of instability
(regardless of symptoms)2
C1-C2 Fusion
C1 fixation options: sublaminar wires, lateral mass screws (in patients older than 2 years)24
(Figure 9)
Vertebral artery at risk with lateral dissection at C1 (Figure 10)
C2 fixation options
Variable course of the vertebral artery and its relationship to the isthmus of C2 are key in the
use of C2 pars screws or pedicle screws.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
16/22

In children with an anomalous vertebral artery course or a sclerotic isthmus that does not
allow screw placement, translaminar C2 screws can be used for rigid fixation without placing
the vertebral artery at risk of injury.24
Figure 9 Lateral radiograph of an upper cervical spine demonstrates reduction and adequate
alignment 1 year after instrumented C1-C2 fusion with iliac crest autograft. (Reproduced
from Hedequist DJ, Emans JB: Cervical spine instrumentation in children. J Am Acad Orthop
Surg 2016;24[6]:370-378.)
Figure 10 Three-dimensional CT angiograms of the cervical spine show the course of the
vertebral artery. A, Posterior view shows the course of the vertebral artery (arrow) as it exits

9/3/26, 5:35 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059

the skull and traverses the C1 ring. B, Oblique view of a duplicate scan shows the relationship
of the vertebral artery (arrow) with C1, C2, and the subaxial cervical vertebra. (Reproduced
from Hedequist DJ, Emans JB: Cervical spine instrumentation in children. J Am Acad Orthop
Surg 2016;24[6]:370-378.)
C1-C2 transarticular (Magerl) screws (Figure 11)
Requires extensive preoperative radiologic evaluation including fine-slice (1-mm) CT scans with
multiplanar reconstruction to evaluate the anatomy of the C1-2 joint space
Can be used only if C1-C2 is reduced; very technically demanding placement
Follows trajectory of C2 pars screws
Figure 11 Computer-generated illustration of a cervical spine shows the path of a
transarticular screw. Note the position of the vertebral artery in relation to the screw path. A
C2 pars screw follows the same trajectory but stops short of the C1-C2 joint. (Reproduced from
Hedequist DJ, Emans JB: Cervical spine instrumentation in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2016;24[6]:370-378.) 
Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Cervical Spine Abnormalities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001059
18/22

Risk of injury to the vertebral artery can be minimized via thorough understanding of the
anatomy and meticulous dissection. 26
Nonunion and a mortality rate as high as 25% are reported with C1-C2 fusion in patients with
Down syndrome.
Subaxial Screw Placement
At C3 through C6, lateral mass screws usually are used because of the small size of the
pedicles and the small corridors between the spinal cord and the vertebral arteries.
At C7, lateral mass anatomy usually is not optimal for screw fixation, but pedicle anatomy
allows for pedicle screw placement.24
Complications
Injury to nerve roots
Vertebral artery and venous plexus injury may occur with wide dissection.
May lose subaxial cervical spine lordosis if posterior musculature is dissociated
Mark as Complete
